analysis.one_liner: Blocks the EPA from banning freon in home, car, and farm air conditioners.
analysis.headline: The freon bill, introduced with no cosponsors, sat in a House subcommittee and died without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped the Environmental Protection Agency from banning or phasing out CFC-12 (freon) for car and farm air conditioners and HCFC-22 for home air conditioners. It would also wipe out any existing EPA rules that restrict those chemicals, and it would have done so even though the phaseout is required by a signed international treaty, the Montreal Protocol. The phaseout existed because these chemicals destroy the ozone layer, which shields people from skin-cancer-causing radiation.
analysis.who_benefits: People and businesses that own or service older air conditioning equipment designed for freon: drivers of older cars, farmers, and repair shops would keep a cheaper, familiar refrigerant. Chemical companies producing CFC-12 and HCFC-22 would keep a legal market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Owners of older AC equipment and repair shops

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit the EPA from banning, phasing out, or restricting freon (CFC-12) for automobile and agricultural air conditioning, or HCFC-22 for residential air conditioning [S2][S3].
It would repeal every existing EPA rule that restricts those chemicals, so owners of older equipment could keep servicing it without converting to newer, more expensive refrigerants [S2][S3].
It would override not just the Clean Air Act but also the Montreal Protocol and related international agreements to which the U.S. is a party [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Everyone shares the cost of continued ozone depletion, including added skin-cancer and cataract risk. Manufacturers and installers who already invested in substitute refrigerants and new equipment would face competing, cheap freon undercutting their products.

drawbacks.text: Freon and HCFC-22 are ozone-depleting chemicals; the phaseout they would preserve was written into the Montreal Protocol to shrink the ozone hole and reduce ultraviolet radiation reaching the ground [S2][S3].

The bill would have the U.S. unilaterally break the terms of an international treaty it signed, undermining an agreement that every industrialized country joined and inviting retaliation or noncompliance by others [S3].
Because the Clean Air Act phaseout was already in force, keeping freon legal would mainly delay the transition already underway, leaving equipment owners facing the switch later at greater expense.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The short-term savings for owners of older air conditioners are real but small and temporary, while the cost is a slower repair of the ozone layer and a unilateral walk-away from a treaty the U.S. helped lead. The bill offered no transition plan or alternative benefit to offset that.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee, then to its Health and Environment Subcommittee, and no one ever brought it up for action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mac Thornberry introduced the bill on November 15, 1995, with no cosponsors [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce, which sent it to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment six days later; no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill would have slowed the freon phaseout, its quiet death in subcommittee left the existing ozone-protection rules intact — to the benefit of public health and the manufacturers who had already converted to substitutes. Owners of older freon equipment did not get the relief the bill promised.

for.name: Rep. Mac Thornberry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to keep freon legal for car, home, and farm air conditioners.

against.name: House Committee on Commerce (104th Congress)
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, passed it to the Health and Environment Subcommittee, and never reported the bill or scheduled any action.

sides.party_line_note: There was no vote and no recorded opposition; the bill's single Republican sponsor drew no cosponsors from either party, and it died quietly in committee [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Producers of CFC-12 and HCFC-22 refrigerant chemicals
industries.note: The bill would have kept legal a market that the Montreal Protocol phaseout was shutting down, preserving revenue from chemicals that deplete the ozone layer. Their gain would come at the cost of slower ozone recovery for everyone.

industries.industry: Manufacturers of substitute refrigerants and new AC equipment
industries.note: Companies that had already invested in ozone-safe refrigerants and redesigned equipment would face continued competition from cheap freon, undermining the transition the bill's rivals had paid to make.

industries.industry: Auto repair and HVAC service shops
industries.note: Shops servicing older cars and home systems would keep access to a cheaper, familiar refrigerant, but the eventual phaseout would return with the conversion bill even larger.
